e-3432.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Curve
e-3432.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y) = x^2 + 2y^2 +x$ that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1, 1).$
e-3432.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y) = (1,1)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(1,1).$  

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y) = (1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+x)\,j \\  & =(2x+0+1)\,i+(0+4y+0)\,j \\  & =(2x+1)\,i+4y\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(2(1)+1)\,i+4(1)\,j \\  & =3\,i+4\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since we want a unit normal vector, we normalize $\nabla f(1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,1)}{‖∇f(1,1)‖} & =\frac{3\,i+4\,j}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(3\,i+4\,j)\end{aligned}
$$

e-3433.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
e-3433.problem: Consider the plane curve $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1.$ Find an equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0, 4).$
e-3433.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16} - 1,$ our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,4)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(0,4).$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{9}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16}-1)j \\  & =\frac{2x}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{8}\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,4) & =\frac{2(0)}{9}\text{ }i+\frac{(4)}{8}\text{ }j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\text{ }j \\  & =⟨0,\,\frac{1}{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,4).$

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf{v} = \langle v_x, v_y \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{x-{x}_{0}}=\frac{{v}_{y}}{{v}_{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

or, equivalently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{y}(x-{x}_{0}) & ={v}_{x}(y-{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(0,4)= \left\langle 0, \:\dfrac12 \right\rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(x-0) & =0(y-4) \\ \frac{1}{2}x & =0 \\ x & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we conclude that the equation of the normal line to the ellipse $\dfrac{x^2}9 + \dfrac {y^2}{16}=1$ at the point $(0,4)$ is $x=0.$

e-3434.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface
e-3434.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z) = 2x^2 - xy - z^2,$ find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$
e-3434.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)$ can be found by computing 
$\nabla f(2, 3, \sqrt 2).$   

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(2{x}^{2}-xy-{z}^{2})\text{ }k \\  & =(4x-y)\text{ }i-x\text{ }j-2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,3,\sqrt{2}) & =(4\cdot 2-3)\text{ }i-2\text{ }j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k \\  & =5i-2j-2\sqrt{2}\text{ }k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $5 \mathbf i  - 2 \mathbf j - 2 \sqrt 2\ \mathbf k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z) = (2, 3, \sqrt 2).$

e-3435.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
e-3435.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $z = \ln (x^2 - xy)$ at the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right).$
e-3435.worked_solution:
To find the equation of the normal line, we first find the equation of a normal vector, and then write the equation of the line that is parallel to the normal vector.

To obtain a normal vector, we write our curve as a level curve and then compute the gradient. Bringing all the terms of our equation to one side, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy) \\ 0 & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z) = \ln (x^2 - xy) - z,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $\left(2, 1, \ln 2 \right)$ can be found by computing $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2){:}$  

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-xy)-z)k \\  & =(\frac{2x-y}{{x}^{2}-xy})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{y-x})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\ ∇f(2,1,\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & =(\frac{2\cdot 2-1}{{2}^{2}-2\cdot 1})\text{ }i+(\frac{1}{1-2})\text{ }j-\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{3}{2}i-\,j-k \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2},-1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, remember that the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\mathbf v = \langle v_x, v_y, v_z \rangle$ and passes through the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, writing the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $\nabla f(2,1,\ln 2)= \left\langle  \dfrac {3} {2}, -1, -1\right  \rangle,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-2}{(\frac{3}{2})}=\frac{y-1}{-1}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-1} \\ \frac{x-2}{3}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$, can be found by computing $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j \\ ∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) & =2(-\frac{1}{2})\text{ }i+2(\frac{1}{2})\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})}{‖∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})‖} & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function f(x,y)=x2+y2 that passes through the point where (x,y)=(−12,12).

a
−22(i−j)
b
−j
c
−22(i+j)
d
−12(i−j)
e
i
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where (x,y)=(−12,12), can be found by computing ∇f(−12,12).

So, we first find the gradient of f(x,y) and evaluate it at (x,y)=(−12,12):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(x2+y2) i+∂∂y(x2+y2) j=2x i+2y j∇f(−12,12)=2(−12) i+2(12) j=−i+j

Finally, we normalize ∇f(−12,12):

∇f(−12,12)‖∇f(−12,12)‖=−i+j(−1)2+(1)2=−i+j2=−22(i−j)

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option a: ∇f(-1/2,1/2)=-i+j, whose magnitude is √2. Normalizing gives -(√2/2)(i-j). The displayed incorrect result concerns the submitted option e, not option a.

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Curve
content.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$
content.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$, can be found by computing $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\text{ }j \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j \\ ∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}) & =2(-\frac{1}{2})\text{ }i+2(\frac{1}{2})\text{ }j \\  & =-i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})}{‖∇f(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})‖} & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-i+j}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i-j)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,1).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point  where $(x,y)=(1,1)$, can be found by computing $∇g(1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & ={g}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{g}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y\,i+\frac{1}{xy}\cdot x\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j \\ ∇g(1,1) & =\frac{1}{(1)}\,i+\frac{1}{(1)}\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇g(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇g(1,1)}{‖∇g(1,1)‖} & =\frac{i+j}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}

Question 2

Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function g(x,y)=ln⁡(xy) that passes through the point where (x,y)=(1,1).

a
22(i−j)
b
3(i+j)
c
32(i−j)
d
22(i+j)
e
i+j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where (x,y)=(1,1), can be found by computing ∇g(1,1).

So, we first find the gradient of g(x,y) and evaluate it at (x,y)=(1,1):

∇g(x,y)=gx(x,y)i+gy(x,y)j=∂∂x(ln⁡(xy))i+∂∂y(ln⁡(xy))j=1xy⋅yi+1xy⋅xj=1xi+1yj∇g(1,1)=1(1)i+1(1)j=i+j

Finally, we normalize ∇g(1,1):

∇g(1,1)‖∇g(1,1)‖=i+j12+12=22(i+j)

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Curve
content.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $g(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy)$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,1).$
content.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point  where $(x,y)=(1,1)$, can be found by computing $∇g(1,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & ={g}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{g}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xy))\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{xy}\cdot y\,i+\frac{1}{xy}\cdot x\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j \\ ∇g(1,1) & =\frac{1}{(1)}\,i+\frac{1}{(1)}\,j \\  & =i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇g(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇g(1,1)}{‖∇g(1,1)‖} & =\frac{i+j}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y}$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(1,4).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(x,y)=(1,4)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,4).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x}+2\sqrt{y})\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{y}}\,j \\ ∇f(1,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}\,i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{4}}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,i+\frac{1}{2}\,j \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(1,4):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(1,4)}{‖∇f(1,4)‖} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2}(i+j)}{‖\frac{1}{2}(i+j)‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}})}\cdot \frac{1}{2}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j).\end{aligned}
$$

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (x,y)=(1,4) can be found by computing ∇f(1,4).

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}+x+y$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,0).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(0,0)$, can be found by computing $∇f(0,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{x+y}+x+y)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{x+y}+x+y)\text{ }j \\  & =({e}^{x+y}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{x+y}+1)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(0,0) & =({e}^{0+0}+1)\text{ }i+({e}^{0+0}+1)\text{ }j \\  & =2i+2j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we normalize $∇f(0,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∇f(0,0)}{‖∇f(0,0)‖} & =\frac{2i+2j}{\sqrt{(2)^{2}+(2)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2i+2j}{2\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Find a unit normal vector to the level curve of the function $f(x,y)=x+3y-2xy$ that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point where $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1)$, can be found by computing $∇f(\frac{3}{2},1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at $(x,y)=(\frac{3}{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+3y-2xy)\text{ }j \\  & =(1-2y)\text{ }i+(3-2x)\text{ }j \\ ∇f(\frac{3}{2},1) & =(1-2(1))\text{ }i+(3-2(\frac{3}{2}))\text{ }j \\  & =-i\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)=2xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,1).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-2y)\,i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-2x)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(0))\,j \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,1)=⟨-1,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1} & =\frac{y-1}{1} \\ -x & =y-1 \\ x+y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Consider the plane curve ln⁡(x+y)=2xy. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (0,1).

a
x+2y−2=0
b
x+y+1=0
c
x−y+1=0
d
x+y−1=0
e
−x+y−1=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: ln⁡(x+y)=2xyln⁡(x+y)−2xy=0

If we set f(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y)−2xy, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (0,1) can be found by computing ∇f(0,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (0,1):

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(ln⁡(x+y)−2xy)i+∂∂y(ln⁡(x+y)−2xy)j=(1x+y−2y)i+(1x+y−2x)j∇f(0,1)=(10+1−2(1))i+(10+1−2(0))j=−i+j=⟨−1,1⟩

Hence, ∇f(0,1)=⟨−1,1⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (0,1).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−0−1=y−11−x=y−1x+y−1=0

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
content.problem: Consider the plane curve $\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)=2xy.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,1).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =2xy \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2xy)\,j \\  & =(\frac{1}{x+y}-2y)\,i+(\frac{1}{x+y}-2x)\,j \\ ∇f(0,1) & =(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(1))\,i+(\frac{1}{0+1}-2(0))\,j \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,1)=⟨-1,1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{-1} & =\frac{y-1}{1} \\ -x & =y-1 \\ x+y-1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Set F(x,y)=2xy+6y²-x+2. Its gradient at (8,-3) is (2y-1,2x+12y)=(-7,-20), giving the normal line direction. Thus 7(y+3)=20(x-8), which simplifies to -20x+7y+181=0, option a.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Consider the plane curve $2xy+6{y}^{2}=x-2.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(8,-3).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy+6{y}^{2} & =x-2 \\ 2xy+6{y}^{2}-x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2xy+6{y}^{2}-x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(8,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(8,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(8,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+6{y}^{2}-x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+6{y}^{2}-x)\,j \\  & =(2y-1)\,i+(2x+12y)\,j \\ ∇f(8,-3) & =(2(-3)-1)\,i+(2(8)+12(-3))\,j \\  & =-7\,i-20\,j \\  & =⟨-7,-20⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 Hence, $∇f(8,-3)=⟨-7,-20⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(8,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: 

$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
content.problem: Consider the plane curve $2xy+6{y}^{2}=x-2.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(8,-3).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy+6{y}^{2} & =x-2 \\ 2xy+6{y}^{2}-x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=2xy+6{y}^{2}-x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$   

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(8,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(8,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(8,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+6{y}^{2}-x)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+6{y}^{2}-x)\,j \\  & =(2y-1)\,i+(2x+12y)\,j \\ ∇f(8,-3) & =(2(-3)-1)\,i+(2(8)+12(-3))\,j \\  & =-7\,i-20\,j \\  & =⟨-7,-20⟩\end{aligned}
$$

 Hence, $∇f(8,-3)=⟨-7,-20⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(8,-3).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-8}{-7} & =\frac{y-(-3)}{-20} \\ -20(x-8) & =-7(y+3) \\ -20x+7y+160+21 & =0 \\ -20x+7y+181 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: 6xy=5x2+y20=5x2+y2−6xy

If we set f(x,y)=5x2+y2−6xy, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=0.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (1,1) can be found by computing ∇f(1,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (1,1):

∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(5x2+y2−6xy)i+∂∂y(5x2+y2−6xy)j=(10x−6y)i+(2y−6x)j∇f(1,1)=(10−6(1))i+(2(1)−6)j=4i−4j=⟨4,−4⟩

Hence, ∇f(1,1)=⟨4,−4⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (1,1).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−14=y−1−4x−1=−y+1x+y−2=0

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
content.problem: Consider the plane curve $6xy=5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(1,1).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}6xy & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} \\ 0 & =5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=0.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(1,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-6xy)\,j \\  & =(10x-6y)\,i+(2y-6x)\,j \\ ∇f(1,1) & =(10-6(1))\,i+(2(1)-6)\,j \\  & =4\,i-4\,j \\  & =⟨4,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(1,1)=⟨4,-4⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(1,1).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-1}{4} & =\frac{y-1}{-4} \\ x-1 & =-y+1 \\ x+y-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Set F(x,y)=√(x²+y²)-2y+x+2. At (0,2), ∇F=(x/√(x²+y²)+1,y/√(x²+y²)-2)=(1,-1). The normal line through (0,2) therefore satisfies y-2=-x, or x+y=2.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Consider the plane curve $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=2y-x-2.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,2).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =2y-x-2 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+1)i+(\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2)j \\ ∇f(0,2) & =(\frac{0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}+1)i+(\frac{2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}-2)j \\  & =i-j \\  & =⟨1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,2)=⟨1,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,2).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{-1} \\ x & =2-y \\ x+y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the plane curve x2+y2=2y−x−2. Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point (0,2).

a
2x−y=−2
b
x+y=2
c
3x+y=2
d
x−y=−2
e
3x+2y=4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: x2+y2=2y−x−2x2+y2−2y+x=−2

If we set f(x,y)=x2+y2−2y+x, our curve can be viewed as the level curve f(x,y)=−2.

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point (0,2) can be found by computing ∇f(0,2).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (0,2): ∇f(x,y)=fx(x,y)i+fy(x,y)j=∂∂x(x2+y2−2y+x)i+∂∂y(x2+y2−2y+x)j=(xx2+y2+1)i+(yx2+y2−2)j∇f(0,2)=(002+22+1)i+(202+22−2)j=i−j=⟨1,−1⟩

Hence, ∇f(0,2)=⟨1,−1⟩ is a normal vector to the curve at (0,2).

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vyx−01=y−2−1x=2−yx+y=2

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms the normal direction is (1,-1). The line through (0,2) with this direction is y-2=-x, hence x+y=2, option b. The incorrect submission was option d, which has slope +1.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
content.problem: Consider the plane curve $\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}=2y-x-2.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(0,2).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & =2y-x-2 \\ \sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=-2.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(0,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(0,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(0,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2y+x)j \\  & =(\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+1)i+(\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2)j \\ ∇f(0,2) & =(\frac{0}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}+1)i+(\frac{2}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}}}-2)j \\  & =i-j \\  & =⟨1,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(0,2)=⟨1,-1⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(0,2).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}} & =\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}} \\ \frac{x-0}{1} & =\frac{y-2}{-1} \\ x & =2-y \\ x+y & =2\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 10
after.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$
after.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=4.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =2(2)\,i+2(0)\,j \\  & =4\,i \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨4,0⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-2)0-(y-0)4 & =0 \\ -4y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0) can be written as:

(x−x0)vy−(y−y0)vx=0(x−2)0−(y−0)4=0−4y=0y=0

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Plane Curve Using the Gradient
content.problem: Consider the plane curve ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.$  Find the equation of the normal line to the curve at the point $(2,0).$
content.worked_solution:
If we set $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, our curve can be viewed as the level curve $f(x,y)=4.$  

A normal vector to the level curve that passes through the point $(2,0)$ can be found by computing $∇f(2,0).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & ={f}_{x}(x,y)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y)\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇f(2,0) & =2(2)\,i+2(0)\,j \\  & =4\,i \\  & =⟨4,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $∇f(2,0)=⟨4,0⟩$ is a normal vector to the curve at $(2,0).$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-{x}_{0}){v}_{y}-(y-{y}_{0}){v}_{x} & =0 \\ (x-2)0-(y-0)4 & =0 \\ -4y & =0 \\ y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The gradient is ∇f=(x,y,z)/√(x²+y²+z²). At (3,4,0), it equals (3/5,4/5,0), which is perpendicular to the level surface. Thus option d is valid; any nonzero scalar multiple is also normal.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

Question 11
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0).

a
45i+35j
b
35i+45j+k
c
35i+45j+15k
d
35i+45j
e
i+j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0) can be found by computing ∇f(3,4,0).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(3,4,0):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2+y2+z2)i+∂∂y(x2+y2+z2)j+∂∂z(x2+y2+z2)k=xx2+y2+z2 i+yx2+y2+z2 j+zx2+y2+z2 k∇f(3,4,0)=3(3)2+(4)2+(0)2i+4(3)2+(4)2+(0)2j+0(3)2+(4)2+(0)2k=35i+45j

Therefore, 35i+45j is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(3,4,0).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface
content.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$
content.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(3,4,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}})\,k \\  & =\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }i+\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }j+\frac{z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\text{ }k \\ ∇f(3,4,0) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,i+\frac{4}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,j+\frac{0}{\sqrt{(3)^{2}+(4)^{2}+(0)^{2}}}\,k \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\frac{3}{5}\,i+\frac{4}{5}\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(3,4,0).$

a
−2i+2k
b
2i+2k

decision.explanation: The gradient ∇f=(2x,2y,2z) is perpendicular to the level surface. At (-1,0,1), it equals (-2,0,2)=-2i+2k, option a. Any nonzero scalar multiple is also a normal vector.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-1,0,1).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =2x\text{ }i+2y\text{ }j+2z\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,0,1) & =2(-1)\,i+2(0)\,j+2(1)\,k \\  & =-2\,i+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $-2\,i+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,0,1).$

Question 12
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,0,1).

a
−2i+2k
b
2i+2k
c
−2i+k
d
−2i−j+2k
e
−2i+j+2k
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,0,1) can be found by computing ∇f(−1,0,1).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(−1,0,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(x2+y2+z2)i+∂∂y(x2+y2+z2)j+∂∂z(x2+y2+z2)k=2x i+2y j+2z k∇f(−1,0,1)=2(−1)i+2(0)j+2(1)k=−2i+2k

Therefore, −2i+2k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,0,1).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms ∇f(-1,0,1)=(-2,0,2), so option a is perpendicular to the level surface. Any nonzero scalar multiple also works. Submitted option e has a nonzero j component and is not parallel to the gradient.

Question 13
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=xy2+yz2+x2z, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,1,−1).

a
3i−j−k
b
i−j−3k
c
−3i−j−2k
d
3i−j−4k
e
3i−j−2k
Submit

decision.explanation: ∇f=(y²+2xz,2xy+z²,2yz+x²). At (-1,1,-1), this equals (3,-1,-1), so option a is perpendicular to the level surface. Any nonzero scalar multiple is also a normal vector.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-1,1,-1).$  

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$  and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,k \\  & =({y}^{2}+2xz)\text{ }i+(2xy+{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2yz+{x}^{2})\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,1,-1) & =((1)^{2}+2(-1)(-1))\,i+(2(-1)(1)+(-1)^{2}))\,j+(2(1)(-1)+(-1)^{2})\,k \\  & =3\,i-1j-1\,k\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $3\,i-\,j-\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1).$

For the function f(x,y,z)=xy2+yz2+x2z, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,1,−1).

a
3i−j−k
b
i−j−3k
c
−3i−j−2k
d
3i−j−4k
e
3i−j−2k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(−1,1,−1) can be found by computing ∇f(−1,1,−1).

So, we first find the gradient of f(x,y,z) and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(−1,1,−1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(xy2+yz2+x2z)i+∂∂y(xy2+yz2+x2z)j+∂∂z(xy2+yz2+x2z)k=(y2+2xz) i+(2xy+z2) j+(2yz+x2) k∇f(−1,1,−1)=((1)2+2(−1)(−1))i+(2(−1)(1)+(−1)2))j+(2(1)(−1)+(−1)2)k=3i−1j−1k

content.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1).$
content.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(-1,1,-1).$  

So, we first find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$  and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}z)\,k \\  & =({y}^{2}+2xz)\text{ }i+(2xy+{z}^{2})\text{ }j+(2yz+{x}^{2})\text{ }k \\ ∇f(-1,1,-1) & =((1)^{2}+2(-1)(-1))\,i+(2(-1)(1)+(-1)^{2}))\,j+(2(1)(-1)+(-1)^{2})\,k \\  & =3\,i-1j-1\,k\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{3}+{z}^{2}{y}^{2}+2z)\,k \\  & =3{x}^{2}\text{ }i+2{z}^{2}y\text{ }j+(2z{y}^{2}+2)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-1,-1) & =3(1)^{2}\,i+2(-1)^{2}(-1)\,j+(2(-1)(-1)^{2}+2)k \\  & =3\,i-2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $3\,i-2\,j$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,-1).$

after.name: Question 15
after.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$
after.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,k \\  & =-\frac{y}{{z}^{2}-xy}\text{ }i+(-\frac{x}{{z}^{2}-xy}-z)\text{ }j+(\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}-xy}-y)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =-\frac{(-2)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}\,i+(-\frac{1}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-0)\,j+(\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-(-2))\,k \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$

Question 15
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(z2−xy)−yz, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−2,0).

a
i−12j
b
i−12j+12k
c
−i−12j+2k
d
i−12j+2k
e
i−2j+2k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−2,0) can be found by computing ∇f(1,−2,0).

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at (x,y,z)=(1,−2,0):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(ln⁡(z2−xy)−yz)i+∂∂y(ln⁡(z2−xy)−yz)j+∂∂z(ln⁡(z2−xy)−yz)k=−yz2−xy i+(−xz2−xy−z) j+(2zz2−xy−y) k∇f(1,−2,0)=−(−2)(0)2−(1)(−2)i+(−1(0)2−(1)(−2)−0)j+(2(0)(0)2−(1)(−2)−(−2))k=i−12j+2k

Therefore, i−12j+2k is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where (x,y,z)=(1,−2,0).

content.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Level Surface
content.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz$, find a vector that's perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$
content.worked_solution:
A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0)$ can be found by computing 
$∇f(1,-2,0).$ 

So, we first find the gradient and evaluate it at $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{2}-xy)-yz)\,k \\  & =-\frac{y}{{z}^{2}-xy}\text{ }i+(-\frac{x}{{z}^{2}-xy}-z)\text{ }j+(\frac{2z}{{z}^{2}-xy}-y)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,-2,0) & =-\frac{(-2)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}\,i+(-\frac{1}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-0)\,j+(\frac{2(0)}{(0)^{2}-(1)(-2)}-(-2))\,k \\  & =i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $i-\frac{1}{2}\,j+2\,k$ is perpendicular to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-2,0).$

Question 16
?

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface 3x2−xz=6−3xyz at the point (1,0,−3).

a
x−19=y−9=z−3−1
b
x−19=y−9=z+3−1
c
x−19=y−9=z−3
d
x−19=y9=z+3
e
x−19=y9=z+3−1
Submit

decision.explanation: Set F=3x²-xz+3xyz-6. Its gradient is (6x-z+3yz,3xz,-x+3xy), which at (1,0,-3) equals (9,-9,-1). The normal line through that point therefore has symmetric equation (x-1)/9=y/(-9)=(z+3)/(-1), option b.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $3{x}^{2}-xz=6-3xyz$ at the point $(1,0,-3).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-xz & =6-3xyz \\ 3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz & =6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)k \\  & =(6x-z+3yz)\text{ }i+3xz\text{ }j+(-x+3xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,-3) & =(6(1)-(-3)+3(0)(-3))\text{ }i+3(1)(-3)\text{ }j+(-1+3(1)(0))\text{ }k \\  & =9\,i-9\,j-k \\  & =⟨9,-9,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{9}=\frac{y-0}{-9}=\frac{z-(-3)}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{9}=\frac{y}{-9}=\frac{z+3}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (1,0,−3):

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
content.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $3{x}^{2}-xz=6-3xyz$ at the point $(1,0,-3).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-xz & =6-3xyz \\ 3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz & =6\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)=3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=6.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,0,-3)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,0,-3).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,0,-3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(3{x}^{2}-xz+3xyz)k \\  & =(6x-z+3yz)\text{ }i+3xz\text{ }j+(-x+3xy)\text{ }k \\ ∇f(1,0,-3) & =(6(1)-(-3)+3(0)(-3))\text{ }i+3(1)(-3)\text{ }j+(-1+3(1)(0))\text{ }k \\  & =9\,i-9\,j-k \\  & =⟨9,-9,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-1}{9}=\frac{y-0}{-9}=\frac{z-(-3)}{-1} \\ \frac{x-1}{9}=\frac{y}{-9}=\frac{z+3}{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface x=y2−z2 at the point (3,2,1).

a
 x−3=y−22=z−1
b
 x−32=y−24=z−1
c
 x−14=2−y=z−1
d
x−1=y−2=z−1
e
 x−3=2−y4=z−12
Submit

decision.explanation: Set F=x-y²+z². Then ∇F(3,2,1)=(1,-4,2). The normal line through (3,2,1) is (x-3)/1=(y-2)/(-4)=(z-1)/2, equivalent to option e.

after.name: Question 18
after.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 18
?

Find the equation of the normal line to the surface x=y2−z2 at the point (3,2,1).

a
 x−3=y−22=z−1
b
 x−32=y−24=z−1
c
 x−14=2−y=z−1
d
x−1=y−2=z−1
e
 x−3=2−y4=z−12
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: x=y2−z2y2−z2−x=0

If we set f(x,y,z)=y2−z2−x, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=0.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (3,2,1) can be found by computing ∇f(3,2,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (3,2,1):

∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(y2−z2−x)i+∂∂y(y2−z2−x)j+∂∂z(y2−z2−x)k=−i+2yj−2zk∇f(3,2,1)=−i+2(2)j−2(1)k=−i+4j−2k=⟨−1,4,−2⟩

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to v=⟨vx,vy,vz⟩ and passes through the point (x0,y0,z0) can be written as:

x−x0vx=y−y0vy=z−z0vzx−3(−1)=y−24=z−1(−2)x−31=y−2−4=z−12x−3=2−y4=z−12

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms the normal vector is (-1,4,-2), equivalently (1,-4,2). Through (3,2,1), this gives x-3=(2-y)/4=(z-1)/2, option e. Submitted option b has direction (2,4,1), which is not parallel to the normal.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
content.problem: Find the equation of the normal line to the surface $x={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(3,2,1).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={y}^{2}-{z}^{2} \\ {y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x & =0\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x$, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(3,2,1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(3,2,1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(3,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}-{z}^{2}-x)k \\  & =-i+2y\,j-2z\,k \\ ∇f(3,2,1) & =-i+2(2)\,j-2(1)\,k \\  & =-i+4\,j-2\,k \\  & =⟨-1,4,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the Cartesian equation of the line that is parallel to $v=⟨{v}_{x},{v}_{y},{v}_{z}⟩$ and passes through the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-{x}_{0}}{{v}_{x}}=\frac{y-{y}_{0}}{{v}_{y}}=\frac{z-{z}_{0}}{{v}_{z}} \\ \frac{x-3}{(-1)}=\frac{y-2}{4}=\frac{z-1}{(-2)} \\ \frac{x-3}{1}=\frac{y-2}{-4}=\frac{z-1}{2} \\ x-3=\frac{2-y}{4}=\frac{z-1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface z2sin⁡(x2y)=x2z+y−π2 at the point (−1,π2,1).

a
 ⟨2,−1,1⟩+t⟨−1,π2,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
 ⟨−1,π2,1⟩+t⟨1,1,−1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
 ⟨−1,π2,1⟩+t⟨2,−1,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
 ⟨−1,π2,1⟩+t⟨2,1,−1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
 ⟨2,1,−1⟩+t⟨−1,π2,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit

decision.explanation: Set F=z²sin(x²y)-x²z-y+π/2. Its gradient is (2xyz²cos(x²y)-2xz, x²z²cos(x²y)-1, 2zsin(x²y)-x²). At (-1,π/2,1), this equals (2,-1,1). The normal line is the given point plus t times this gradient, matching option c.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}z+y-\frac{\pi }{2}$ at the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1).$
after.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}z+y-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)k \\  & =(2xy{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2xz)i+({x}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-1)j+(2z\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2})k \\ ∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =(2(-1)(\frac{\pi }{2})(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-2(-1)(1))i+((-1)^{2}(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-(-1)^{2})k \\  & =(-\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+2)i+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)k \\  & =2\,i-j+k \\  & =⟨2,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ and passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)=⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,⟨2,-1,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Question 19
?

Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface z2sin⁡(x2y)=x2z+y−π2 at the point (−1,π2,1).

a
 ⟨2,−1,1⟩+t⟨−1,π2,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
b
 ⟨−1,π2,1⟩+t⟨1,1,−1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
c
 ⟨−1,π2,1⟩+t⟨2,−1,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
d
 ⟨−1,π2,1⟩+t⟨2,1,−1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
e
 ⟨2,1,−1⟩+t⟨−1,π2,1⟩,t∈(−∞,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we bring all variables to one side: z2sin⁡(x2y)=x2z+y−π2z2sin⁡(x2y)−x2z−y=−π2

If we set f(x,y,z)=z2sin⁡(x2y)−x2z−y, our surface can be viewed as the level surface f(x,y,z)=−π2.

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point (−1,π2,1) can be found by computing ∇f(−1,π2,1).

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (−1,π2,1): ∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(z2sin⁡(x2y)−x2z−y)i+∂∂y(z2sin⁡(x2y)−x2z−y)j+∂∂z(z2sin⁡(x2y)−x2z−y)k=(2xyz2cos⁡(x2y)−2xz)i+(x2z2cos⁡(x2y)−1)j+(2zsin⁡(x2y)−x2)k∇f(−1,π2,1)=(2(−1)(π2)(1)2cos⁡((−1)2π2)−2(−1)(1))i+((−1)2(1)2cos⁡((−1)2π2)−1)j+(2(1)sin⁡((−1)2π2)−(−1)2)k=(−πcos⁡(π2)+2)i+(cos⁡(π2)−1)j+(2sin⁡(π2)−1)k=2i−j+k=⟨2,−1,1⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(−1,π2,1) and passes through the point (−1,π2,1) can be written as

r=⟨−1,π2,1⟩+t∇f(−1,π2,1)=⟨−1,π2,1⟩+t⟨2,−1,1⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of the Normal Line to a Surface Using the Gradient
content.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}z+y-\frac{\pi }{2}$ at the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1).$
content.worked_solution:
First, we bring all variables to one side:

$$
\begin{aligned}{z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y) & ={x}^{2}z+y-\frac{\pi }{2} \\ {z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

If we set $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y,$ our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-\frac{\pi }{2}.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be found by computing $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({z}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2}z-y)k \\  & =(2xy{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-2xz)i+({x}^{2}{z}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}y)-1)j+(2z\operatorname{sin}⁡({x}^{2}y)-{x}^{2})k \\ ∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1) & =(2(-1)(\frac{\pi }{2})(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-2(-1)(1))i+((-1)^{2}(1)^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2(1)\operatorname{sin}⁡((-1)^{2}\frac{\pi }{2})-(-1)^{2})k \\  & =(-\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+2)i+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)j+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-1)k \\  & =2\,i-j+k \\  & =⟨2,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ and passes through the point $(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,∇f(-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1)=⟨-1,\frac{\pi }{2},1⟩+t\,⟨2,-1,1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at (−1,π2,1): ∇f(x,y,z)=fx(x,y,z)i+fy(x,y,z) j+fz(x,y,z) k=∂∂x(z2sin⁡(x2y)−x2z−y)i+∂∂y(z2sin⁡(x2y)−x2z−y)j+∂∂z(z2sin⁡(x2y)−x2z−y)k=(2xyz2cos⁡(x2y)−2xz)i+(x2z2cos⁡(x2y)−1)j+(2zsin⁡(x2y)−x2)k∇f(−1,π2,1)=(2(−1)(π2)(1)2cos⁡((−1)2π2)−2(−1)(1))i+((−1)2(1)2cos⁡((−1)2π2)−1)j+(2(1)sin⁡((−1)2π2)−(−1)2)k=(−πcos⁡(π2)+2)i+(cos⁡(π2)−1)j+(2sin⁡(π2)−1)k=2i−j+k=⟨2,−1,1⟩

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to ∇f(−1,π2,1) and passes through the point (−1,π2,1) can be written as

r=⟨−1,π2,1⟩+t∇f(−1,π2,1)=⟨−1,π2,1⟩+t⟨2,−1,1⟩, where t∈(−∞,∞).

decision.explanation: For F=x²y+y²z+z²x, ∇F=(2xy+z²,x²+2yz,y²+2zx). At (1,-1,2), this is (2,-3,5). The normal line is the given point plus t times this gradient, matching option b.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem: Find a vector equation of the normal line to the surface ${x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x=5$ at the point $(1,-1,2).$
after.worked_solution:
Let's set $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x.$ Then, our surface can be viewed as the level surface $f(x,y,z)=5.$ 

A normal vector to the level surface that passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be found by computing $∇f(1,-1,2).$ 

So, we find the gradient and evaluate it at $(1,-1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & ={f}_{x}(x,y,z)\,i+{f}_{y}(x,y,z)\text{ }j+{f}_{z}(x,y,z)\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}y+{y}^{2}z+{z}^{2}x)k \\  & =(2xy+{z}^{2})\,i+({x}^{2}+2yz)\,j+({y}^{2}+2zx)\,k \\ ∇f(1,-1,2) & =(2(1)(-1)+(2)^{2})\text{ }i+((1)^{2}+2(-1)(2))\text{ }j+((-1)^{2}+2(2)(1))\text{ }k \\  & =2\,i-3\,j+5\,k \\  & =⟨2,-3,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the vector equation of the line that is parallel to $∇f(1,-1,2)$ and passes through the point $(1,-1,2)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,∇f(1,-1,2)=⟨1,-1,2⟩+t\,⟨2,-3,5⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$
